extracted.intended_audience: general public and media professionals interested in newsroom ethics and standards
extracted.subtask_description: A news article reporting on internal newsroom dispute and the ethical/procedural questions it raises about investigative reporting, leak probes, and newsroom culture. Focuses on what constitutes appropriate handling of sensitive reporting and internal dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of internal materials
rubrics_metrics.description: "Revealing editing drafts, reporter notes or other confidential materials to outside media erodes trust and undermines our culture of collaboration,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal drafts, reporter notes, planning documents and draft scripts should be treated as confidential; leaking such materials to outside outlets is framed as harmful to newsroom trust and collaboration. The article treats protection of unpublished work and internal deliberations as a core newsroom standard and justification for a leak investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-discrimination in investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: "No one in our newsroom or company has been or will be scrutinized because of ethnic or national origin... Any such thing would be deeply offensive to us and the Guild's accusation is wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations into leaks or internal dissent must not target or single out staffers on the basis of ethnic or national origin. The union's grievance alleges 'targeted interrogation' of journalists of Middle Eastern descent; management denies this. Guidance implies investigatory procedures should avoid ethnic profiling and respect anti-discrimination commitments in contract and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid questioning staff about employee-group participation or political views
rubrics_metrics.description: The guild said members "faced extensive questions about the involvement in [Middle Eastern North African employee group] events and discussions and about their views of the Times' Middle East coverage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line of questioning that probes staff participation in identity-based employee groups or asks about personal views of coverage risks being perceived as discriminatory or retaliatory; such questioning should be avoided or handled with clear necessity and safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust verification for sensitive allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: As Times audio producers ... questioned how solid the underlying evidence was that their colleagues had gathered; critics argued the anecdotes weren't fully nailed down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of sexual violence and other highly sensitive allegations require especially strong corroboration. Before producing additional content (e.g., podcasts) or amplifying a report, producers should confirm the solidity of evidence and verify anecdotes to avoid harm and error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up substantiation and willingness to correct
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporting team acknowledged concerns about the story and sought to offer further substantiation in a follow-up piece involving an investigation by the United Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When questions arise about reporting, news organizations should pursue follow-up reporting and independent corroboration (e.g., external investigations) and be prepared to correct, clarify, or qualify earlier accounts if new information undermines them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of contributors' prior public conduct while judging work on its merits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Intercept noted social media postings of a freelancer; Times International Editor said, "She made valuable contributions and we saw no evidence of bias in her work..." and termed prior social media posts "unacceptable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past social-media conduct by freelancers or reporters may be relevant and draw scrutiny, but editors must distinguish between prior personal posts and demonstrated bias in reporting. The article presents both concerns about appearance and the newsroom's statement defending the reportage's accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality of staff who voiced doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: The guild said reporters were asked to turn over confidential communications and which colleagues had voiced doubts about the original report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should avoid compelling employees to identify colleagues who expressed internal doubts; protecting the confidentiality of internal critique helps preserve a culture where staff can raise concerns without fear of reprisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from prior major retractions — rigorous source vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: In late 2020, The Times was compelled to retract the core of an investigative podcast series ... when the fantastical claims of its key source unraveled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past high-profile failures (e.g., retractions driven by unreliable sources) imply a need for stricter vetting of key sources and skepticism toward narratives built on single, uncorroborated accounts—especially for immersive audio or long-form projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide internal channels for airing misgivings
rubrics_metrics.description: He wrote that the paper had expanded ways for journalists at the newspaper to share misgivings and concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should create and publicize multiple mechanisms for staff to raise concerns internally (editing reviews, ombudspersons, formal complaint processes) as alternatives to public disclosure, to surface problems while limiting harmful leaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage conflicts of interest and recusal policies for visible staff activism
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Los Angeles Times ... the then top editor barred reporters who signed such protest letters from covering the conflict for three months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporters take public positions (e.g., sign protest letters), newsrooms may impose temporary reassignment or recusal from related beats to manage perceived conflicts of interest and preserve credibility; policies should be transparent and proportionate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial purpose: inform the present rather than predict history's judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher A.G. Sulzberger: 'Journalists don't serve the public by trying to predict history's judgments, or to steer society to them... Our job as journalists is firmly rooted in the present: to arm society with the information and context it needs to thoughtfully grapple with issues of the day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should prioritize accurate, contextual information for the present public debate rather than attempting to shape or pre-judge how history will view events; this principle guides choices about tone, framing, and stakes in contentious coverage.
